#5233. AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

#5232. What Is Backpack Crypto? BP Explodes 30% After CFTC Approval

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

First, what is Backpack crypto? Why is it exploding? Backpack is suddenly becoming one of the market’s hottest stories after securing a major regulatory breakthrough in the United States. Its native BP token surged 30% in 24 hours as traders rushed to price in the exchange’s latest expansion. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has effectively opened the door for Backpack to challenge established crypto derivatives platforms on American soil.

The approval gives Backpack the regulatory foundation to operate a US derivatives exchange and clearinghouse. Its ambitions extend beyond simply offering another place to trade Bitcoin and Ethereum. The company wants to combine leveraged crypto trading, collateral management, and global liquidity under one regulated platform.

The development also arrives as competition heats up over who can deliver the next generation of crypto trading infrastructure.

Founded by Armani Ferrante, Backpack started as a Solana-focused crypto wallet and exchange. It has since expanded into securities, tokenization, and derivatives. The company then reports more than $450 billion in cumulative trading volume and customers across over 150 countries.

Its latest breakthrough involves two separate approvals from the CFTC. The Designated Contract Market (DCM) registration allows Backpack to operate a regulated derivatives exchange.

Backpack is coming home to the USA. 🇺🇸We’ve received landmark CFTC approval to establish the first-ever derivatives exchange powered by one order book with unified global liquidity.Leveraged perpetuals. Crypto collateral. Cross-margin. 24/7 trading.Join the waitlist:…

Meanwhile, its Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO) registration provides the infrastructure needed to manage collateral, margin, and settlement obligations. Together, these approvals establish the foundation for Backpack to offer leveraged crypto perpetual futures in the United States.

The proposed platform will support 24/7 trading, crypto and fiat collateral, cross-margining, and access to Backpack’s global order book.

That last feature could prove particularly important. Rather than isolating American traders inside a separate liquidity pool, Backpack wants to connect US customers with its international trading ecosystem.

BP responded immediately. The token climbed by more than 30% over 24 hours to $1.10, pushing its market cap higher as trading activity accelerated. The rally ties to growing expectations that Backpack could become a serious competitor in the American derivatives market.

The regulatory breakthrough also strengthens its position against offshore platforms that have dominated leveraged crypto trading for years.

Backpack’s approval exposes an interesting opportunity across the wider crypto market. Bitcoin remains the industry’s largest liquidity pool, yet its base layer was never designed for sophisticated smart contracts, high-speed decentralized trading or complex margin products.

That creates an infrastructure gap developers are racing to fill. Solana demonstrated how quickly decentralized applications can execute transactions. Bitcoin, meanwhile, offers a much deeper pool of established capital.

Bringing those strengths together could unlock an entirely different market for Bitcoin-denominated trading.

Projects exploring this direction, Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER), which combines Bitcoin Layer 2 infrastructure with Solana Virtual Machine technology. Its architecture aims to let users bridge BTC into a faster environment supporting smart contracts and decentralized applications.

The potential goes beyond faster transfers. Bitcoin liquidity could eventually support decentralized spot markets, margin trading, and perpetual futures without forcing traders to abandon Bitcoin for another blockchain ecosystem.

Bitcoin Hyper has already attracted more than $33.2 million through its presale, exceeding Backpack’s previously disclosed $17 million Series A funding round. Its token currently sells for just $0.0137, while its staking program advertises rewards of up to 35% APY.

With its November 26 launch target approaching, the presale is entering its final stretch. The combination of Bitcoin liquidity and Solana-style execution is attracting attention as developers look for ways to bring more sophisticated financial applications to Bitcoin.

Backpack now has something many offshore competitors cannot easily replicate: a regulatory pathway into the American derivatives market. The company still needs to turn its approvals into actual trading activity, but the potential market is enormous.

American traders represent an important source of institutional and retail liquidity. Bringing them into a unified order book could strengthen Backpack’s competitive position while attracting market makers and professional trading firms.

BP’s 30% rally shows investors are already anticipating that expansion, and Backpack’s regulatory breakthrough could mark the beginning of a much larger shift in crypto trading.

The race is no longer just about building another exchange. It is about connecting deeper liquidity, faster execution, and increasingly sophisticated financial products. Bitcoin’s enormous capital base makes that opportunity particularly difficult to ignore.

#5230. Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say

It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.

“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”

Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”

It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)

Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

#5229. Tokenized Stocks Open 24/7 on OKXICE, but Only Crypto Firms Signed Up: Will Wall Street Follow?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. OKXICE, the joint venture of crypto exchange OKX and NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), opens round-the-clock trading in tokenized stocks for eligible US customers on Sunday, November 23. The only companies whose shares it will offer at launch are crypto firms: Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, Strategy, BitGo and Securitize.

Of the 62 companies the venue first picked, 56 objected. Its November 5 notice lists 67 objectors in all, including every member of the Magnificent Seven.

⚡️JUST IN: OKX and NYSE parent ICE will launch 24/7 tokenized U.S. securities trading on November 23 through their joint venture, OKXICE.More than 70 assets are expected, including Coinbase, Circle, Robinhood, and Strategy securities, plus 59 Direxion ETFs.The platform will… pic.twitter.com/TfRuuZrcV0

That leaves buyers with a narrow menu. We checked what they will actually get: the six stocks are down a median 42% this year, while the S&P 500 is up 7%. Five of the six have moved more closely with Bitcoin than the S&P 500 has over the past three months.

The launch is the first real test of a new SEC rule meant to bring listed shares onto blockchains. So will Wall Street follow, or is this a crypto-only market for now?

Explore: Will Tokenized Stocks Move by xStocks Bring New Volume to HSBC, Shell and Other European Equities?

A tokenized stock is a blockchain token that tracks a listed share. ICE set up the venture after it invested in OKX in March at a $25 billion valuation. On OKXICE, each token is backed by a real US share, and customers hold it in a self-custody wallet inside the OKX app.

The venue runs under an exemption the SEC issued on September 17. It lets blockchain venues trade tokenized versions of listed US shares without registering as an exchange, for up to five years. Companies are not asked to opt in. Instead, each one gets 30 days after being notified to object, and silence counts as consent.

Most said no. Applied Optoelectronics said it was worried about pricing, liquidity and volatility, and that investors might think it backed the product. The OKXICE launch page confirms the November 23 start, with more than 70 assets, 59 of them exchange-traded funds from Direxion.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

We pulled daily prices for the six launch stocks from Yahoo Finance. Then we measured how far each has moved in 2026 and how closely its daily moves tracked Bitcoin over the past 90 trading days.

So a US investor who wanted Apple or Nvidia around the clock gets, for now, five stocks that rise and fall with the crypto market. ICE’s own shares, by comparison, are up 8% this year and barely track Bitcoin at all, with a correlation of 0.08.

The objections don’t mean Wall Street is ignoring tokenization. It is building its own version first.

In March, the SEC approved a Nasdaq pilot that puts tokenized and regular shares in the same order book. The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), which settles most US stock trades, runs a tokenization service with 20 participants and 34 securities. In September, Nasdaq agreed to invest $100 million in Payward, the parent of crypto exchange Kraken, to build infrastructure for tokenized shares.

The difference is control. In those projects, exchanges and clearing houses run the system, and trading stays tied to regular market hours and rules. OKXICE offers 24/7 trading, which companies have pushed back on: a share that trades all weekend leaves no quiet time to handle bad news. Nasdaq has also warned that splitting trading across separate venues could thin out liquidity.

So the answer is “not yet.” Wall Street is likely to reach tokenized stocks through its own exchanges and DTCC before it lets crypto venues list its shares.

Robinhood is the launch name with the most at stake: it already sells tokenized stocks to European customers. Its 24/7 contract on Hyperliquid, a crypto exchange that lists perpetual futures on US stocks, trades at $70.32.

On the daily chart, HOOD sits far below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $90.17, and its 200-day EMA at $97.99.

XYZ:HOODUSD 1D chart. Source: Hyperliquid

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

The number to watch after Sunday is not OKXICE’s volume but its objection list. The first large non-crypto company to stay off it would be the clearest sign that Wall Street is ready to follow tokenized stocks onto a crypto venue.

Institutional demand has offered little immediate relief. U.S. spot Ether ETFs recorded $398.9 million in weekly outflows between November 9 and 13, adding another source of pressure.

Now, the North Korean hacker’s enormous Ethereum holdings introduce another uncomfortable variable. The $1,800 level has become an important psychological battleground. Losing it again could expose ETH to another round of panic selling, particularly if traders begin pricing in the possibility of additional stolen funds entering the market.

#5226. Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending

Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”

That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra. If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor, Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”

Bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself — for example, when Tal Lavin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”

“AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”

This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

“E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”

So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

Flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries.

The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Ranganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

“We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.”

Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project, with the campaign ending on November 27.

#5225. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

#5224. Satoshi’s Bitcoin DNA in XRP Ledger Uncovered in Two Cryptographic Mechanisms

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

XRP Ledger Foundation Director of Community Hussein Zangana (Vet) shared a tidbit of XRPL's early history in a recent X post.

Vet noted that the XRP Ledger (XRPL) still carries traces of Satoshi Nakamoto’s original Bitcoin design, highlighting two features.

In 2011, three engineers—David Schwartz, Jed McCaleb, and Arthur Britto—began developing the XRP Ledger (XRPL). Fascinated by Bitcoin, they set out to create a better version that improved upon its limitations—with the goal of creating a digital asset that was more sustainable and built specifically for payments.

As reported, the first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written by David Schwartz, who is Ripple CTO emeritus, about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011.

Vet delves into the earliest part of XRP Ledger history, noting that 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, wrote. Vet added that Jed McCaleb also copied Satoshi’s timekeeping code into the XRPL, even including one of the Bitcoin creator’s comments shared as a screenshot.

Did you know all of us on the XRP Ledger use design choices by Satoshi daily? 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Satoshi wrote. Jed copied Satoshi's timekeeping code into the XRPL, including one of Satoshi's comments. By the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone. In December 2014, Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment. Two design choices of Satoshi still remain on the XRPL and all of us use at least one of it. Signature curve secp256k1 (we also support Ed25519 thus not everyone uses this) and how XRPL addresses are generated from the public key with SHA-256 followed by RIPEMD-160, that's what all of us use.

The quote "Never go to sea with two chronometers; take one or three" is a classic maritime adage famously included by Satoshi Nakamoto (the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin) within the Bitcoin source code.

Vet explained that by the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone from the XRP Ledger. In December 2014, former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment.

However, two of Satoshi's design choices still remain on the XRP Ledger: the first is the secp256k1 signature curve, which Bitcoin uses and which the XRP Ledger continues to support. However, the ledger also supports Ed25519, meaning not every XRPL user relies on secp256k1.

"I remember David saying they used secp256k1 so no one would doubt the security because it's the same as Bitcoin's, etc.," Vet stated, citing the insight of the Ripple CTO emeritus on secp256k1, adding, "Lots of interesting things to dig into from the early days."

The second is the method used to generate XRP Ledger addresses from public keys. The process applies SHA-256 hashing followed by RIPEMD-160, a design inherited from Bitcoin that remains common to all XRPL addresses.

Asked why the timekeeping code and Satoshi's comment were removed, Vet explained that this became leftover code as new code was introduced, so it was cleaned up.

#5223. Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market

Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indusbridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.

In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

Wall Street is getting closer to Solana, and this time, it isn’t just buying tokens; it could change the direction of its price prediction. Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), the owner of the New York Stock Exchange, is considering operating a Solana validator. This arrives as Solana officially graduates from its Mainnet Beta era.

Yet SOL holders aren’t exactly celebrating as the token remains deep in correction territory after falling from its September highs at $125. With Wall Street knocking on Solana’s door, holders now face a tempting question: Is a $90 recovery finally coming, or does SOL have another painful trip toward $60?

ICE is considering operating a Solana validator, according to comments from ICE Clear Europe President Hester Serafini at Solana Breakpoint in London yesterday. Validators help secure Solana’s network and participate in transaction processing and consensus. Having one of the world’s largest financial market operators participate could strengthen Solana’s institutional credibility.

ICE is already preparing for a closer relationship with the blockchain. Its planned tokenized securities trading infrastructure can accept tokens minted on Solana. The company hasn’t confirmed a validator launch, but the possibility puts Solana firmly on Wall Street’s radar.

🔥MASSIVE: ICE Clear Europe President Hester Serafini says NYSE parent ICE is already working with Solana and exploring becoming a validator."There's a number of things we're already working on, and we're quite keen to explore more things going forward," Serafini reveals. pic.twitter.com/4c8clIw8Wt

Yesterday at Breakpoint, Solana officially left beta. The transition marks years of Solana’s development as the network moves toward a more mature production environment. Its Alpenglow upgrade targets 150-millisecond transaction finality, while Firedancer introduces another independently developed validator client.

In other words, Solana isn’t just chasing faster transactions anymore. It’s positioning itself as infrastructure for financial markets that cannot afford to move at internet meme speed.

Solana has upgraded, but another project is trying to bring its speed to Bitcoin without leaving Bitcoin’s liquidity behind. Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is building a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by the Solana Virtual Machine (SVM), combining high-speed execution with access to Bitcoin-based liquidity.

The project has already raised more than $33.2 million, while HYPER remains available at just $0.0136877 per token. That’s barely above one cent, with the presale approaching its scheduled November 26 closing date.

Staking adds another incentive. Bitcoin Hyper offers a 35% APY for participants locking their tokens through its buy-and-stake option.

While Solana continues building its institutional presence, Bitcoin Hyper is pursuing a different opportunity: bringing Solana-style execution to Bitcoin’s enormous liquidity ecosystem. With more than $33 million already committed and the presale countdown approaching its final days, HYPER is positioning itself for attention ahead of its scheduled launch.

Here’s where things get interesting. Despite the institutional headlines, SOL remains considerably weaker than its September performance. The token has dropped from $125, leaving buyers scrambling to defend the $70 region.

The daily Relative Strength Index has also entered deeply oversold territory, displaying that sellers may have exhausted much of their immediate momentum. But this also creates an interesting setup for a potential relief rally.

The first challenge sits around $74–$75. Reclaiming this area could bring $80 into view, where bulls need a convincing breakout before targeting $89–$90. A successful recovery toward $90 would show a meaningful reversal from the recent lows. It would also give investors a reason to believe institutional adoption is finally influencing market sentiment.

However, the bears haven’t disappeared. Losing the $70 support region could expose SOL to another wave of selling. The next major downside target sits around $60, potentially wiping out another chunk of investor confidence.

The institutional story gives Solana a compelling long-term narrative. ICE’s potential validator participation, DTCC’s tokenization plans, and the network’s latest upgrade all strengthen its position in the race for blockchain-based financial infrastructure. But the market still needs Solana to deliver the money before a bullish price prediction.

Cardano DReps have rejected a proposal by Toto Finance to spend 22 million ADA from the Cardano treasury on a "Strategic Copper Reserve."

The vote closed on Nov. 15, and DReps holding 2.86 billion ADA voted against the proposal, according to Cardano governance data. DReps with 20.02 million ADA voted in favor of it.

DRep John MacPherson was among those who voted "No," and he explained his decision in a post on X.

MacPherson wrote that he is not against real-world assets on Cardano. Still, he said the proposal asks the treasury "to take on both the copper price and the ada price," and Toto Finance would collect "up to about 3.4M ada in fees."

At the same time, MacPherson said that the proposal is “more honest about its risks than most.”

Toto Finance, a company led by Monty Metzger, submitted the proposal on Oct. 15. ADA is trading at $0.152 on Monday, and the requested 22 million ADA is now worth around $3.3 million.

The plan was to buy copper with 14.72 million ADA and store it in a warehouse near New Orleans. Toto Finance wanted to issue one CuTT token for each pound of copper. The metal would be sold in 18 to 24 months.

The Cardano Foundation, which votes as a DRep, announced its "No" vote in October.

"We recognize the opportunity in real-world asset tokenization; however, this proposal places 22,000,000 ada under the recipient's sole control to fund a fee-heavy concentrated commodity position whose safeguards are not yet in place," the foundation wrote.

Three members of the Constitutional Committee voted "No," and the other four members did not vote.

Crypto commentator Ingeniero Cripto agreed with MacPherson in the replies under his post. He called the "double exposure" to the prices of copper and ADA the key problem of the proposal, as the Cardano treasury already holds ADA.

According to him, RWAs on Cardano make sense, but “funding the asset itself is a different question than funding the rails.”

#5220. ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and issues shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration shows how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 new shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS says the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets quickly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a plan as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For users, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

#5219. Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

The funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”

Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he said, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.

Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows users to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

#5218. Binance’s Co-Founder Says Crypto Market Pullback Is Temporary

Yi He, the co-founder of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has sparked discussions across the crypto market after urging retail traders to stay calm even as major crypto assets continue to post massive daily losses.

Yi He’s consoling statement has come as crypto traders grow increasingly weary and the prolonged market volatility begins to cause even bigger losses, with Bitcoin retesting $63,000.

In her post, Yi urged investors holding major crypto assets that have been substantially affected by the severe market volatility to remain calm amid the latest market downturn.

She described the ongoing crypto market pullback as ‘temporary’ while assuring spot traders that they have little reason to worry.

Alongside the post, Yi He shared a link to the Binance app showcasing a 30-day asset change of approximately -$101.31 million in her account.

The figure indicates the amount of losses the pro-crypto investor has suffered on her holdings over a period of about a month, from October 17 to November 16, 2026.

Although the showcased portfolio shows a decline in the founder’s holdings, it does not establish whether the decline represents realized trading losses, unrealized losses, withdrawals, or other changes in Yi He’s account.

It appears that some investors may have found comfort in Yi He's message as they expressed support, noting that turbulent conditions like these don’t necessarily last long.

However, other commentators have questioned whether wealthy industry figures like Yi He can fully understand the financial pressure facing retail traders at a time like this.

Some of the arguments questioned how meaningful such reassurance could be for retail investors, arguing that losing 100 million yuan might not significantly affect someone with substantial wealth like her.

Meanwhile, a loss of 20,000 or 30,000 yuan could wipe out an ordinary investor's savings.

Publicly listed Bitcoin miners have sold nearly half of their Bitcoin since January. Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode published the report today, November 18. The miners are using the coins to pay for a move into AI data centers. Its chart of six miners, led by MARA Holdings, shows combined holdings falling from about 110,000 BTC early this year, with the biggest monthly drop coming in November.

Bitcoin miners are rapidly selling their reserves.For years, listed miners held what they mined, and some bought more. Since January, they have sold nearly half their bitcoin:native.A major shift in their approach: the BTC now funds their move into AI data centers. pic.twitter.com/Pe3bE0YJ19

For years, these companies held what they mined, and some bought more. That made them steady holders in the Bitcoin market. Now they are sellers, at a time when the price is already down 28% this year.

We used these data to check whether the switch helped shareholders of these Bitcoin miners. Four of the six stocks fell more than Bitcoin this year, with a median loss of 41%. Only Riot Platforms and Hut 8 are up.

So who is selling, and what does it mean for the Bitcoin price?

Discover: Tokenized Stocks Open 24/7 on OKXICE, but Only Crypto Firms Signed Up: Will Wall Street Follow?

Glassnode tracks the Bitcoin that six listed miners report holding: MARA Holdings, Riot Platforms, CleanSpark, Hut 8, American Bitcoin and Cango. From 2021 to late 2025, their combined stack only grew. This year, it has shrunk in most months, and November’s drop is the largest on the chart.

MARA, the largest holder, accounts for most of it. Its latest filing shows it sold 13,597 BTC for about $1.1 billion over six weeks, at an average price of about $81,000. It used $750 million to repay a loan backed by its Bitcoin and said it would keep selling to build cash for AI infrastructure.

The reason is money. Since the April 2024 halving, each block pays half as much Bitcoin, and the price has fallen from its peak. Renting power and buildings to AI companies pays steadier income, and the coins on the balance sheet are the fastest way to fund the switch.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

We compared each company’s share price this year with Bitcoin’s 28% drop, using Yahoo Finance daily closes from January 2 to November 17.

MARA’s timing looks better than its stock. It sold at about $81,000 on average, roughly 27% above Bitcoin’s $63,947 today.

Sales by Bitcoin miners add supply, but MARA’s $1.1 billion over six weeks is small next to a market worth about $1.3 trillion. The bigger change is in behavior: a group that used to soak up coins now sells them.

That matters most when demand is weak, as it is now. The Fear & Greed Index, a daily sentiment gauge from 0 to 100, sits at 11, in “extreme fear.” Each miner sale adds to the coins buyers have to absorb.

On the daily chart, Bitcoin trades at $63,947. Its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, has just slipped below its 200-day EMA, at about $75,750 each. Traders call that a “death cross,” a sign that the longer downtrend is taking over.

Bitcoin miners won’t go back to hoarding soon. The AI build-out needs cash for years, and their coins are the cheapest source of it. The next sign to watch is December’s holdings data, which will show whether November was a one-off or the new normal.

#5215. After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

It’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.

ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined company will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.

But the EV market didn’t take off as quickly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.)

Part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the company spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet big on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products.

Many new grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the company that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery company I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

My recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz said ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz said.

Currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz said the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”

Today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is currently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

In its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The company said it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”

ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.

But it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the company has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.

#5214. After 7 Years and 99% Speed Leap, Solana (SOL) Finally Drops Its 'Beta' Label

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Solana has officially removed the "beta" tag from its mainnet's name and introduced the Solana 1.0 standard. The switch was announced on Nov. 16 at the Breakpoint conference in London.

"Solana 1.0 marks the network's graduation from 'mainnet beta' to 'mainnet,' retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch," the Solana Foundation said.

Solana launched on March 16, 2020, and the network had been working under the "mainnet-beta" label for six years and eight months. According to the foundation, the label "never evolved to signal its production status."

The Solana Foundation coordinated the rollout with the Anza and Firedancer teams. Co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko replied to the announcement on X with three exploding-head emojis.

"For users, this is the same network, nothing changes. Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same," the foundation wrote. On Monday, SOL is trading at $71.35.

According to the foundation, two upgrades made the change possible. In October, Solana activated Alpenglow with the Agave 4.3 release, and the time to final confirmation went down by almost 99%, from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds.

Firedancer, a validator client developed by Jump Crypto independently from Agave, is also now running on the Solana mainnet. Independent implementations "limit the impact of bugs affecting one client, and strengthen network resilience," the foundation said.

Solana 1.0 also gives the network a shared protocol version, and it does not depend on the version numbers of individual clients such as Agave and Firedancer.

"A shared protocol version lets everyone refer to Solana's evolution without using one client's release number as shorthand for the entire network," the Solana Foundation explained. "Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once."

Earlier this year, Solana raised the compute limit per block from 60 million to 100 million compute units in May, and the slot time went down from 400 to 200 milliseconds in August. The maximum transaction size also went up from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes.

"Documentation, websites, explorers, and other ecosystem surfaces will progressively reflect the updated designation," the foundation added.

#5213. Claude AI Predicts LIT Rebound Following Lighter Crypto Hack

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Forget the temporary dip tied to yesterday’s exploit. By New Year’s Day 2027, Anthropic’s Claude AI predicts Lighter crypto will deliver one of the sharpest post-incident rebounds the perp DEX sector has seen this cycle, the kind of violent recovery that turns a scary headline into pure rocket fuel.

The LIT price took a hit on yesterday’s exploit news, dropping more than 20% to $2.50. However, the team’s response and USDC fund recovery have seen the price recover to just under $3, surging +10% over the past 24 hours.

On November 16, 2026, Lighter, the high-performance decentralized perpetuals exchange that settles on Ethereum with zero-knowledge proofs, activated Guardian mode and paused all withdrawals and new pool creation.

On-chain data showed roughly $10.39M in USDC leaving the platform’s Ethereum settlement contract in a single withdrawal. Some researchers put the total impact closer to $15.5M across two large market-maker accounts. The attacker used a leaked API key tied to a trader’s account. The root cause was insecure custom signing code that reused cryptographic nonces, allowing the attacker to reconstruct the private key from public signatures.

With the key, the attacker created a public pool from the compromised account, acquired most of its shares, moved the victim’s USDC into the pool, and redeemed it. Importantly, Lighter’s core protocol and smart contracts were never compromised; this was an account-level key compromise, not a smart-contract exploit. Funds were rapidly swapped into ETH, with portions routed to Hyperliquid. LIT initially dropped by 20% on the news before buyers stepped in.

BREAKING: Hackers steal nearly $15.5 MILLION from Lighter using leaked API keys.$LIT crashed 18% on the news. pic.twitter.com/Rf2PsTSSRd

Lighter moved fast. Within hours, the team publicly confirmed the cause, named the attacker wallet, and made clear that the protocol itself remained intact. The Security Council recovered approximately $5M in USDC and returned it to the affected trader. Guardian mode was deactivated the same day and withdrawals resumed. New safeguards followed immediately: wallet signatures are now required for transfers into public pools, API key signatures are non-public, IP allowlists are planned, per-key permission limits are in place, and automated monitoring for nonce reuse is active.

Users running custom or third-party signing software were strongly advised to rotate keys and switch to Lighter’s official SDKs. The message was clear: the platform treated the incident as a user-key hygiene issue and hardened the surrounding controls without ever having a core vulnerability.

That combination of transparent communication, partial recovery, rapid resumption of operations, and concrete security upgrades is exactly the kind of response that historically flips sentiment from fear to “they handled it cleanly.”

LIT is currently trading in the $2.65–$3.00 zone after the sharp post-incident flush. The sell-off created a classic higher-volume capitulation low, with RSI on the daily timeframe dipping into oversold territory before printing a higher low.

Price is now reclaiming short-term moving averages while volume has expanded on the green candles, classic signs of aggressive dip-buying rather than distribution. On the higher timeframe, the broader structure remains constructive: a multi-month base that previously supported a run toward the $5+ region is still intact.

A sustained hold above the $2.80–$3.00 recovery zone would open measured-move targets that align with a full post-incident squeeze, especially if volume continues to confirm and the security narrative solidifies. The setup favors a sharp mean-reversion rally once the “protocol was never broken” story fully digests.

#5212. Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

Behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

The Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a new Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

The model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab says it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card shows 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

The two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

Elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

Output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each new token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

The vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

This release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.
