#5046. Bitcoin launches Testnet5 and gives miners a real trial of four proposed fixes

Bitcoin’s new Testnet5 lets miners test four proposed consensus rule changes as Bitcoin Core and Sparrow Wallet prepare support.

Bitcoin miners have a new network, Testnet5, where they can test their software against four proposed changes to Bitcoin’s rules, with support in Bitcoin Core and Sparrow Wallet at the patch stage.

The Bitcoin Improvement Proposals repository added the record of Testnet5’s first block to the network specification on Nov. 17, three days after the block was mined.

The four changes are collectively known as BIP54, or Consensus Cleanup. Bitcoin Inquisition’s signet already enforces them, but producing blocks there also requires miners to satisfy a signing challenge in addition to proof of work.

On Testnet5, independent miners and pools can use their own software to build blocks and see whether other nodes accept them without that extra requirement.

Two of the four rules limit how much work certain blocks can impose on nodes and how miners can use timestamps to influence difficulty. One caps certain signature operations in ordinary transactions to limit how long a block can take to verify.

The other restricts timestamps at the start and end of each difficulty period to prevent miners from artificially driving the difficulty down.

A third rule rejects transactions that measure exactly 64 bytes after removing witness data, closing an ambiguity in proofs of transaction inclusion. The fourth makes each new mining reward transaction unique by requiring its locktime to equal the block height minus one and requiring that locktime to take effect.

Pool operators can use Testnet5 to check that their software, which usually builds the reward transaction, applies the new rule.

Testnet5 enforces four proposed rules from block one, including a new check on the reward transaction that mining pools usually build.

Mining pools can check how their own software builds blocks that meet the proposed rules.

The diagram summarizes Testnet5 rules from block one. Mainnet activation would be separate. Block segment sizes are illustrative.

Diagram groups the four rules by the block data they constrain. The order follows a block’s header and transaction list, starting with the mining reward transaction.

The diagram summarizes Testnet5 rules from block one. Mainnet activation would be separate. Block segment sizes are illustrative.

Testnet4 let miners drop to minimum difficulty if a block’s timestamp was more than 20 minutes after the previous one, except at the start of a difficulty period. BIP95 says competing blocks mined under the exception caused frequent short reorganizations, where one set of recent blocks replaced another.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Testnet5 removes the 20-minute rule altogether and raises the minimum difficulty from 1 to about 1 million. The specification’s authors chose the higher floor to slow early block production before difficulty adjusts, while keeping it low enough for a single specialized mining machine to keep the test chain running.

Early testers can build the Bitcoin Core patch and sync by manually connecting to a peer, its author reported. The proposal targets Core’s 32.x branch and still needs to be merged and shipped in a public release.

Bitcoin Core 32.1, the latest release as of Nov. 18, predates the Testnet5 integration build.

Sparrow’s wallet integration proposal opened late on Nov. 17, and would let users select Testnet5 in the wallet and add two public Electrum servers to connect to the chain.

A Sparrow collaborator reported on Nov. 18 that the wallet’s Silent Payments feature worked in tests against both servers. The proposal, which depends on an update to Sparrow’s Drongo library, remained open.

#5045. Morning Minute: The CFTC Officially Greenlights Perps in the US, Starting with Backpack

Morning Minute: The CFTC Officially Greenlights Perps in the US, Starting with Backpack

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🏛️ Backpack and tZERO Win the First Onchain Derivatives Approvals

For years, perps were the product American traders couldn’t legally touch. On Monday, that officially changed.

Chairman Michael Selig approved applications from Backpack and tZERO to run regulated derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses that execute and settle on blockchain rails. Selig called it “an important milestone in the evolution of American financial markets.”

Backpack got both pieces at once, a Designated Contract Market designation to run the exchange and a Derivatives Clearing Organization registration to clear its own trades. It plans to offer Americans round-the-clock leveraged crypto perps on a single global order book, accepting both fiat and crypto as collateral with cross-margin across positions. tZERO received its exchange approval a week earlier, after already holding clearing registration, and is building it into a derivatives vertical inside its infrastructure business.

Backpack US president Mark Wetjen, himself a former CFTC commissioner, framed it as “moving price discovery from offshore unregulated venues to the United States.” CEO Armani Ferrante said the firm enters markets “fully regulated from day one.” Backpack already runs licensed platforms in Europe, Asia and the UAE.

The CFTC has certainly been busy this month. They cleared single-stock perpetual futures on November 3. It issued guidance on November 5 telling federally regulated exchanges they generally cannot restrict access by state. Now it has approved blockchain-native exchanges and clearinghouses.

Selig is building an onshore home for every product the offshore venues were built to serve, and he is doing it through staff action rather than legislation, with one sitting commissioner and nomination hearings for two more this week.

Hyperliquid is the obvious candidate and also the one that has publicly said it doesn’t want this. Jeff Yan spent his Bloomberg interview this month arguing Hyperliquid is infrastructure rather than an exchange, and that regulators should oversee the firms deploying markets on top rather than the chain underneath. His US route is HIP-3 partners taking on the compliance burden, with ICE investing in Trade.xyz and Kraken’s parent reportedly in talks. Backpack getting a DCM and a DCO makes that argument harder, because it demonstrates a crypto-native venue can simply register.

Then there’s Lighter. It has run Robinhood Wallet’s perps since July on a dedicated instance with a 50/50 revenue split, which is the partner model rather than the registration model. The registered model opens up with a CFTC license, and many think Lighter could very well be next.

One thing’s certain—the CFTC is serious about bringing perps onshore. From Selig himself, “I look forward to building on that milestone.” And we will find out soon enough who’s next…

#5043. Binance Says It Won Court Order to Recover Frozen Hack Funds

Binance says it has secured a court order from Abu Dhabi Global Market to help it recover crypto frozen after the record $6.3 billion hack last month, Reuters reported on Wednesday. The exchange has not said how much of the money the order covers.

Reuters described Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) as Binance’s main financial regulator. Binance deputy general counsel Dugan Bliss confirmed the order in a statement but gave no details on its terms. Neither the company nor Reuters said which assets it applies to.

“We will continue using every lawful tool available to trace, freeze and recover stolen assets, support our partners in returning funds where possible, and keep those assets out of the hands of the attackers,” Bliss said.

Binance has said about $2.85 billion of the stolen tokens were frozen or intercepted after the Oct. 29 attack, according to its own incident report. That is roughly 45% of the $6.34 billion it says was affected.

Most of it sits with stablecoin issuers. Tether said it froze more than $1.5 billion in USDT within 30 minutes of the attack, and Circle said it froze about $1.1 billion in USDC in coordination with law enforcement. Circle added that it does not decide who owns frozen assets, a question it left to law enforcement and the courts.

The Justice Department has separately obtained court authority to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the stolen crypto. It is part of more than $2.7 billion that Justice says government and private-sector efforts have frozen. Criminal Division head A. Tysen Duva said the department helped “immediately halt about half of this historic breach.” Reuters did not say how the ADGM order fits with the U.S. action.

Binance says the attack began months earlier, with a tampered software installer that compromised one engineer in June. In September, another engineer was approached by a fake recruiter and persuaded to run a bogus interview assignment that installed malware, the company said.

From there, the attackers reached an internal wallet-signing service and drained Binance hot wallets across multiple blockchains on Oct. 29. The thefts included 233.46 million XRP, about 970,500 SOL and 18,270 BTC, according to Binance.

The FBI has attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, and Binance has said the same. Pyongyang denies involvement. Blockchain analysts said the attacker tried to outrun the freezes by swapping stablecoins into ether over about 20 minutes, but the issuers moved faster.

That split matters for bitcoin. Tether and Circle can block their own tokens, but bitcoin has no issuer. The stolen BTC is not covered by those freezes and can be stopped only if it reaches an exchange or service that blocks it.

Binance has already said it replaced the affected assets with company funds, using part of its SAFU emergency fund and its corporate treasury. Withdrawals resumed in phases earlier this month, and the exchange aims to reopen all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week, Reuters reported.

On Wednesday, Binance’s Asia-Pacific head SB Seker told Reuters at the Singapore FinTech Festival that the company plans to expand into five Asian markets in 2027 and does not need to raise new funds. He said talks are under way with five or six markets, three of them at a mature stage, and details are due in the first quarter.

Seker said the cost of replacing the stolen tokens was “statistically” not a large amount for the company. “In terms of the impact to us, we can take the impact and we can weather it without any change to the way we operate,” he said.

The initiative plans to initially focus on an intermediated and interoperable stablecoin-based payment model, with participation from borrower countries.

The World Bank Group (WBG) said it is exploring the use of regulated USD stablecoins with Citi and Circle to speed up and cut the cost of fund disbursements.

In a statement released Tuesday, the international organization said that it plans to test blockchain-based payment rails alongside traditional correspondent banking to improve existing WBG funds disbursement arrangements.

"Central to this initiative will be Citi's existing connections to established banking rails and Circle's stablecoin payments infrastructure to mint and settle funds in USDC," the group said.

The initiative is set to build on WBG's existing FundsChain platform, which tracks flows across more than 350 projects in 96 countries. The project plans to initially focus on an intermediated and interoperable stablecoin-based payment model, with participation from borrower countries.

"This initiative is about exploring ways to make the financial plumbing of development work better for the people who need it most," WBG President Ajay Banga said in the statement. "Enabling money to move faster and at lower cost means real development impact – a health clinic gets built on time, a farmer gets paid before the harvest season ends, and a government can be more responsive to pressing needs."

Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said it is building an internet-native financial system, and "development finance is one of its most important applications."

"Money that moves at the speed of the internet shouldn't be reserved for the world's biggest banks and corporations; it should reach the people and places that need it most, with full visibility into where every dollar goes," Allaire added.

The World Bank Group is a multilateral development institution owned by 189 member countries. It comprises five organizations that work to reduce poverty and support sustainable growth in developing economies.

In the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, the group delivered $123.5 billion in loans, grants, equity investments, and guarantees to partner countries and private businesses, according to its latest annual report. This includes $35.8 billion in Sub-Saharan Africa, $25.1 billion in Latin America and the Caribbean, and $24.6 billion in Europe and Central Asia.

#5041. Binance unlocks 20x BlackRock IBIT ETF trades with a weekend catch

Binance's new IBIT futures offer 20x leverage and 24/7 trading, exposing traders to liquidation risks when US markets are closed.

Binance Futures added a perpetual contract tied to BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) on Nov. 18.

The contract (IBITUSDT) gives eligible traders round-the-clock exposure to the Nasdaq-listed fund, settles in Tether’s USDT, and offered up to 20x leverage at launch.

Binance set the opening for 09:45 UTC in a listing notice, and the exchange’s public futures ticker recorded trades after the scheduled opening. The contract keeps trading after the fund’s market closes, and Binance’s mark price can still move far enough to trigger liquidation.

Traders can take a position on IBIT's rise or fall without owning its shares or Bitcoin, as the fund seeks to reflect Bitcoin's price.

Binance’s TradFi FAQ lists the UK, Hong Kong, Taiwan and some European Economic Area countries as common examples of restricted markets for these products. The 20x figure is the launch ceiling, and Binance’s margin rules set lower leverage ceilings for larger positions.

The price index is Binance’s reference for the underlying and helps feed the mark price, the estimate the exchange uses to determine whether a position has reached its liquidation threshold.

During regular equity trading, Binance builds its reference index from third-party price quotes. It smooths those quotes during premarket and after-hours trading, then gives new quotes less weight during the overnight session, according to Binance’s pricing methodology.

On weekends, holidays, and during covered maintenance periods without those quotes, Binance looks to the futures order book, where traders place buy and sell orders for the perpetual.

It averages two measures from that book, the impact bid and impact ask, then smooths the result by giving more weight to recent readings. The index can keep moving while the ETF’s last share price stays where trading left it.

#5039. Standard Life Chair Wants Tokenized Gilts to Open UK Government Bonds to Retail Savers

Standard Life Chair Wants Tokenized Gilts to Open UK Government Bonds to Retail Savers

Tokenization could help ordinary British savers buy government bonds more easily, and should not become a tool only for big financial institutions, according to Sir Nicholas Lyons, chairman of Standard Life.

"Why should it be so unnecessarily complicated for retail investors to buy gilts that fund the nation's needs?" Lyons said at Solana's Breakpoint conference in London.

Lyons, a former Lord Mayor of the City of London whose company has about £480 billion ($633 billion) in assets under administration, said Britain should use tokenization to bring more households into investing. About £850 billion ($1.1 trillion) of household wealth remains in cash, often losing value to inflation, he said.

Tokenization could cut administrative costs, make transfers simpler and let savers invest in small amounts in products that would otherwise be uneconomic, Lyons said. More retail ownership of gilts would make the UK less reliant on foreign buyers and could help erode the risk premium the country has paid on its debt since the September 2022 mini-budget, he added.

The remarks come as the UK prepares to issue its first digitally native government bond, known as DIGIT. Earlier this month, the Treasury confirmed roles for six banks supporting the pilot, with issuance expected in the first quarter of 2027, Lyons said.

"Government bonds sit at the heart of our financial system," he said, noting that they underpin liquidity, provide collateral and set reference rates for other assets. Showing that tokenized gilts can be issued, settled and used as collateral efficiently would lay "an important foundation for much broader digital capital markets," he said.

Lyons credited the Financial Conduct Authority, the Bank of England and the Treasury for progress so far, including the Digital Securities Sandbox and work to let tokenized securities be used as collateral.

The Bank of England has also turned its attention to stablecoins: an executive has said it is treating them as a new form of money, it eased its planned stablecoin rules in June, and it has since been handed a legal duty to foster stablecoin innovation. Lyons cited a July report by Chris Woolard, the government's wholesale digital markets champion, which estimated that faster adoption of digital markets could add as much as £33 billion ($43.5 billion) a year to UK economic output by 2035.

But the competition is moving fast, he warned, pointing to the SEC's innovation exemption for tokenized stock trading in the U.S., and initiatives in Europe, Singapore, Hong Kong, Switzerland and the Middle East.

Lyons set out four priorities: making the digital gilt pilot a success, accelerating tokenized collateral and repo markets, promoting interoperability to avoid "a collection of competing digital platforms that recreate the fragmentation of the existing system," and ensuring retail investors share in the benefits.

He also acknowledged the risks, citing concerns raised by the Financial Times' Gillian Tett that AI-accelerated cyber threats and faster-moving money could fuel a run on deposits. "Tokenization does not automatically make an investment safer, more liquid, or more stable, or suitable for retail investors," he said. "Fractional ownership of a risky asset remains ownership of a risky asset."

"We're not pursuing tokenization for the sake of technological leadership," Lyons said. "We're pursuing better capital markets, more productive investment, greater economic prosperity, and wider participation in the creation of wealth and jobs."

#5036. Scattered Spider Hacker Gets Six Years for $11.6 Million Crypto Theft

A Scottish hacker tied to the Scattered Spider group was sentenced to six years in U.S. federal prison on Tuesday for a text-message phishing and SIM-swapping scheme that stole at least $11.6 million in crypto, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California said.

Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, received a 72-month sentence from U.S. District Judge John W. Holcomb in Santa Ana. He had pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. A restitution hearing is set for Dec. 11.

Prosecutors did not say which cryptocurrencies were taken, and the release does not break the haul down by coin. Buchanan is the fifth and final defendant to be sentenced in the case, closing out a prosecution of a hacker crew that the Justice Department charged together.

From September 2021 to April 2023, Buchanan and his co-conspirators sent hundreds of phishing texts to employees of at least a dozen companies, prosecutors said. The messages posed as the employer or one of its IT contractors and linked to fake login pages that captured usernames, passwords and other personal information.

The group then used the stolen data to run SIM swaps, which move a victim’s phone number to a SIM card the attacker controls. That gave them a way into victims’ virtual currency accounts and wallets. The BBC reported that Buchanan set up a Telegram bot to collect the credentials as workers handed them over.

The largest single theft, according to prosecutors, was $1.67 million taken from one victim in December 2022. Prosecutors said the thefts had “severe, life-altering consequences” for victims.

The BBC said the money came from individual victims rather than from the companies whose employees were phished. Prosecutors first put the hacker group’s take at about $8 million, and the $11.6 million figure is the loss authorities calculated for the full scheme.

Police Scotland searched Buchanan’s bedroom in April 2023 after a request from the FBI, the BBC said. Investigators found a device holding the names and addresses of victims, along with crypto seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.

Buchanan left the U.K. the following month. Spanish authorities arrested him at Palma de Mallorca Airport in 2024 as he tried to board a private flight to Naples.

Bloomberg News reported, and Reuters relayed, that he was extradited from Spain in April 2025. He was charged with wire fraud and aggravated identity theft alongside four other alleged Scattered Spider members, and he has been in U.S. custody since.

Reuters has described Scattered Spider as a loose-knit community of hackers suspected of breaking into dozens of U.S. companies. The DOJ release does not use the group’s name, but the BBC says Buchanan, a teenage hacker when the campaign began, was a member and a Justice Department spokesperson has previously tied the defendants to it.

The BBC said Buchanan’s four co-defendants have all pleaded guilty and are serving time. It described the case as a years-long investigation involving authorities in the U.K., the U.S., Spain and Canada.

Scattered Spider has also faced prosecution in Britain. Two other members were jailed in the U.K. in July for a series of attacks, including one on Transport for London that caused £39 million in damage, the BBC said.

The judge will set the amount of restitution at a hearing on Dec. 11, the final step in the case against the Scottish hacker.

#5035. Invesco moves stablecoin reserves on-chain, but hides a liquidity gap

Invesco's new Ethereum-based stablecoin reserve fund requires institutions to follow business-day redemption schedules.

Invesco announced a government money market fund on Nov. 17 that gives eligible institutions a way to hold part of their stablecoin reserves in fund shares recorded on Ethereum.

If a stablecoin issuer needs dollars from the fund to pay customers, it has to redeem those shares on the fund’s business-day schedule.

The Invesco Stablecoin Reserves Onchain Fund (IROXX) is initially aimed at institutions such as stablecoin issuers and digital asset infrastructure providers. Its shares represent an investment in short-duration US Treasury securities and other eligible reserve assets. Holding a stablecoin alone gives a customer no right to redeem shares in the fund.

Investors in supported jurisdictions need an approved Superstate account and a verified wallet on the allowlist to hold IROXX on the Ethereum network.

The standard initial minimum is $1 million per fund account, and Invesco or an intermediary can combine master accounts and subaccounts to meet it.

To redeem, shareholders submit a request through the Investor Portal run by Superstate, the fund’s sub-transfer agent.

Under the fund’s redemption terms, Superstate normally sends a dollar wire on the next business day if it receives a valid request before 5 p.m. Eastern. For a request received after the cutoff on a business day, the fund normally prices the redemption and sends the wire on the next business day.

The price is the next net asset value per share calculated after Superstate receives the request in good order. The ordinary payment terms allow up to seven days after Superstate receives a request in good order.

Early closes can affect same-day payment, and the fund can also withhold same-day payment in the 30 minutes before it calculates the share price.

A fund business day depends on the New York Fed, the fund’s custodian, and its main portfolio markets being open. Management also has to judge that the market can handle purchase and redemption requests.

Shareholders pay blockchain transaction fees, known as gas, on redemptions. Congestion or insufficient gas can delay a request past the cutoff even if the shareholder starts the transaction before it.

Investors can also elect USDC proceeds through a third-party intermediary, with the service setting its own onboarding and conversion terms, including when it delivers the tokens. The fund’s normal wire schedule gives investors a timetable for when dollars are sent, while USDC delivery depends on the intermediary.
